theorem.statement:
Fix \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\), and put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\},
 \qquad
 \rho=\frac{\nu}{8+4\nu}.
\]
For every fixed \(0<\chi<\rho\), every deterministic integer sequence \(m_n\to\infty\), and every triangular array in \(\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)\), the randomized-jitter Gaussian-multiplier Anderson--Rubin set \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\) is implementable from the stratified observations and independent standard-normal draws and satisfies
\[
 \lim_{n\to\infty}
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \left|
 \Pr_\theta\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\}
 -(1-\alpha_0)
 \right|=0.
\]
This conclusion is uniform over influence covariance matrices whose ranks may change with \(n\), including the zero matrix, and uses neither an inverse nor a positive-eigenvalue bound for that covariance.  The jitter is \(n^{-\chi}\), hence vanishes on the root-\(n\) Anderson--Rubin scale underlying \(\mathcal C_n\).  By contrast, an unrandomized deterministic critical-value rule cannot in general be exactly calibrated at an atom: if the reference statistic has distribution function \(F\), a jump at \(q\), and \(1-\alpha_0\in(F(q-),F(q))\), neither strict nor weak deterministic thresholding at \(q\) has acceptance probability \(1-\alpha_0\).  Thus external randomization, or an assumption excluding such atoms, is necessary for the stated uniform exactness.
theorem.proof_tex:
Write \(W_{e,i}=(T_{e,i},Y_{e,i})\), and let \(q=(E-1)(R_{\max}-d-1)\), which is fixed.  The block maximum norm in the construction is one-Lipschitz with respect to the Euclidean norm.  All constants below depend only on the fixed coefficient, share, calibration-gap, and moment envelopes, never on the member of the triangular array.

At the true value \(b=\beta\), the uniform generated-projector expansion gives
\[
 H_n(\beta)=Z_n+R_n,\qquad
 Z_n=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}),                    \tag{1}
\]
where
\[
 \Sigma_n=\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
 \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^{\top}]
\]
is positive semidefinite and may be singular.  Put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\}>0.
\]
The source moment envelope, the polynomial degree at most \(R_{\max}\) of every cumulant first projection, the coefficient bounds, and
\(\|C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\) imply
\[
 \sup_{n,e,\theta}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|\zeta_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}<\infty.     \tag{2}
\]
Here the displayed division is licensed by the calibration gap
\(\sigma_d(C)\geq\kappa_0>0\), and
\((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\) licenses the moment in (2).

We first record a quantitative form of the singular Gaussian approximation; no covariance inverse is used.  Set
\[
 X_{e,i,n}=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}).
\]
Balanced shares and (2) give
\[
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \mathbb E_\theta\|X_{e,i,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K n^{-\nu/2}.                                 \tag{3}
\]
For a bounded one-Lipschitz function \(f\), convolve \(f\) with a
\(N(0,s^2I_q)\) density and call the result \(f_s\).  Direct
differentiation of that density and the Lipschitz property give
\[
 \|f_s-f\|_\infty\leq K_qs,\qquad
 [D^2f_s]_\nu\leq K_qs^{-1-\nu}.                    \tag{4}
\]
Replace the summands \(X_{e,i,n}\), one at a time, by independent
centered Gaussian vectors with the same covariance.  Taylor's formula
through order two cancels the means and covariances, and its integral
remainder is bounded by
\([D^2f_s]_\nu\|x\|^{2+\nu}/2\).  The Gaussian replacement has
\((2+\nu)\)-moment bounded by a dimension-dependent constant times the
corresponding covariance to the power \(1+\nu/2\), which is bounded by
the right side of (3) by Lyapunov's inequality.  Thus (3)--(4) yield
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L_\theta(Z_n),
 N(0,\Sigma_n)\right)
 \leq K\left(s+n^{-\nu/2}s^{-1-\nu}\right).          \tag{5}
\]
Taking \(s=n^{-\nu/(2(2+\nu))}\) makes the right side
\(O(n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)})\), uniformly, including when \(\Sigma_n\) is
singular.

The proof of the generated-projector expansion also supplies an
explicit rate for its remainder.  The variance of every Hoeffding
projection of order at least two, after multiplication by \(n\), is
\(O(n^{-1})\).  For \(D_n=\widehat C-C\), the projector Taylor
remainder is bounded on
\(\{\|D_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa_0/2\}\) by
\(K\sqrt n\|D_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\), while
\[
 \Pr\{\|D_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}>\kappa_0/2\}
 \leq4\kappa_0^{-2}\mathbb E\|D_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 \leq K/n.                                          \tag{6}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[1\wedge
 \{\sqrt n\|D_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\}\right]
 \leq\sqrt n\,\mathbb E\|D_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
 \leq K n^{-1/2}.                                   \tag{7}
\]
The products of two first-order estimation errors have the same bound
by Cauchy--Schwarz.  Equations (6)--(7), the higher-projection variance
bound, and (1) therefore imply
\[
 \sup_\theta
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L_\theta(H_n(\beta)),
 N(0,\Sigma_n)\right)
 \leq K n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}.                          \tag{8}
\]

We next verify that the multiplier law estimates the possibly singular
Gaussian law.  For an order-\(s\) kernel \(g\), conditional on
\(W_{e,i}\), the first term inside the brackets defining
\(\widehat\psi_{g,e,i}\) is an order-\((s-1)\) \(U\)-statistic for
\(\mathbb E[g(W_{e,i},W_2,\ldots,W_s)\mid W_{e,i}]\).
The overlap count used in the Hoeffding variance calculation and the
uniform square-integrability supplied by the moment envelope give
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \|\widehat\psi_{e,i}-\psi_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2
 =O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})                             \tag{9}
\]
uniformly, after stacking the finitely many cumulant coordinates.
The calibration gap and the projector expansion give
\[
 \|\widehat Q-Q_A\|_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}),
 \qquad
 \|\widehat C^\dagger-C^+\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 =O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2}),                          \tag{10}
\]
and the exceptional branch in the definition of
\(\widehat C^\dagger\) has probability \(O(n^{-1})\) by (6).
Combining (9)--(10) with the bounded population cumulants yields
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{e,i}\pi_e^{-2}
 \|\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)-\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i})\|^2
 =O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1}).                            \tag{11}
\]

Conditionally on the data, \(G_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\) is exactly Gaussian
with covariance
\[
 \widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)
 =
 \frac1n\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \pi_e^{-2}
 \widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)
 \widehat\zeta_{e,i}(\beta)^\top.                   \tag{12}
\]
To control (12) with only the maintained moments, put \(a=\nu/2\).
Each entry of
\(\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^{\top}\) has a uniformly bounded
\((1+a)\)-moment by (2).  Truncate its norm at
\[
 L_n=n^{1/(2(1+a))}.
\]
The truncation bias is at most \(K L_n^{-a}\).  The variance of the
average of the truncated independent matrices is at most
\(K L_n^{1-a}/n\), so its mean absolute deviation is at most
\(K n^{-1/2}L_n^{(1-a)/2}\).  Both terms equal, up to constants,
\[
 n^{-a/(2(1+a))}=n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}.                 \tag{13}
\]
The replacement error in (11) is smaller by Cauchy--Schwarz and the
tightness of the empirical second moments.  Therefore
\[
 \sup_\theta
 \mathbb E_\theta\!\left[
 1\wedge\|\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)-\Sigma_n\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \right]
 \leq K n^{-\nu/(4+2\nu)}.                          \tag{14}
\]

For positive semidefinite matrices, the spectral calculus gives
\[
 \|S^{1/2}-T^{1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \leq\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{1/2}.                   \tag{15}
\]
This follows directly by applying the resolvent identity inside
\[
 S^{1/2}=\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty
 t^{-1/2}S(S+tI)^{-1}\,dt
\]
and splitting the integral at
\(t=\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\); thus (15) remains valid at zero
eigenvalues.  Couple the two Gaussian vectors as
\(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)^{1/2}Z\) and
\(\Sigma_n^{1/2}Z\), where \(Z\sim N(0,I_q)\).  Equations (14)--(15)
and Jensen's inequality give
\[
 \sup_\theta\mathbb E_\theta\!
 \left[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(
 \mathcal L^*(G_n^{*(j)}(\beta)),N(0,\Sigma_n)
 \right)
 \right]
 \leq K n^{-\rho},
 \qquad \rho=\frac{\nu}{8+4\nu}.                    \tag{16}
\]
No rank condition on \(\Sigma_n\) or \(\widehat\Sigma_n(\beta)\) has
entered (12)--(16).

It remains to handle atoms.  Let \(\tau_n=n^{-\chi}\) with
\(0<\chi<\rho\), let \(G_n\sim N(0,\Sigma_n)\), and define the ideal
smoothed distribution function
\[
 F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)
 =
 \Pr\{\|G_n\|_{\max}+\tau_n\xi\leq t\},
 \qquad \xi\sim N(0,1).
\]
For every \(t\), the map
\[
 x\longmapsto
 \Phi\!\left(\frac{t-\|x\|_{\max}}{\tau_n}\right)
\]
is bounded by one and has Lipschitz constant at most
\((\sqrt{2\pi}\tau_n)^{-1}\).  Hence (8) and (16) imply, respectively,
\[
 \sup_{\theta,t}
 \left|
 \Pr_\theta\{V_n(\beta)\leq t\}-F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)
 \right|\longrightarrow0,                          \tag{17}
\]
and
\[
 \sup_\theta\mathbb E_\theta
 \sup_t\left|
 \Pr^*\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\leq t\}
 -F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}(t)
 \right|\longrightarrow0,                          \tag{18}
\]
because the right sides before taking limits are bounded by constants
times \(n^{\chi-\nu/(4+2\nu)}\) and
\(n^{\chi-\rho}\), respectively.  This is precisely why
\(\chi<\rho\) was imposed.

The distribution \(F_{n,\theta}^{\circ}\) is continuous and strictly
increasing even if \(G_n\) is supported on a proper subspace or equals
zero almost surely: its density is
\[
 t\longmapsto
 \mathbb E\left[
 \frac1{\tau_n}
 \phi\!\left(\frac{t-\|G_n\|_{\max}}{\tau_n}\right)
 \right]>0.                                         \tag{19}
\]
Consequently the probability integral transform applied to the ideal
variable has the exact uniform distribution.  The two uniform
Kolmogorov bounds (17)--(18), followed by the elementary inverse-CDF
inequalities, therefore show that the conditional Gaussian upper-tail
probability evaluated at \(V_n(\beta)\) converges in distribution,
uniformly over the shell, to a \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) variable.

Finally, conditional on the data and \(\xi_0\), the \(m_n\) indicators
in \(\widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)\) are independent Bernoulli variables.
If their common success probability is \(p_n^*(\beta)\), then
\[
 \operatorname{Var}\!\left(
 \frac1{m_n}\sum_{j=1}^{m_n}
 \mathbf 1\{V_n^{*(j)}(\beta)\geq V_n(\beta)\}
 \,\middle|\,\text{data},\xi_0
 \right)
 =
 \frac{p_n^*(\beta)\{1-p_n^*(\beta)\}}{m_n}
 \leq\frac1{4m_n}.                                  \tag{20}
\]
Chebyshev's inequality and \(m_n\to\infty\) make the simulated
upper-tail probability differ from \(p_n^*(\beta)\) by
\(o_{\mathbb P}(1)\), uniformly.  Since
\(\alpha_0\in(0,1/2)\) is a continuity point of the uniform law,
(17)--(20) give
\[
 \sup_{\theta\in\mathcal M_r(\lambda_n)}
 \left|
 \Pr_\theta\{\widehat p_{n,m_n}(\beta)>\alpha_0\}
 -(1-\alpha_0)
 \right|\longrightarrow0.                          \tag{21}
\]
By the definition of the inversion set, the event in (21) is exactly
\(\{\beta\in\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\}\), proving the asserted
uniform exact coverage.  Also
\(\tau_n\xi_0=o_{\mathbb P}(1)\), so the randomization vanishes on the
root-\(n\) Anderson--Rubin scale and does not replace the causal target
\(\beta\) by an observable functional.

To prove the obstruction for deterministic critical values, let \(F\)
be any reference distribution with a jump
\(\Delta=F(q)-F(q-)>0\) at \(q\).  Weak deterministic acceptance at
\(q\) has probability \(F(q)\), whereas strict deterministic
acceptance has probability \(F(q-)\).  If
\[
 F(q-)<1-\alpha_0<F(q),
\]
neither rule has the desired acceptance probability.  The explicit
extreme witness is a reference statistic equal to zero almost surely:
every deterministic threshold rule has acceptance probability zero
or one, never \(1-\alpha_0\).  Randomizing acceptance on the equality
event with probability
\[
 \frac{1-\alpha_0-F(q-)}{F(q)-F(q-)}
\]
would repair this atom exactly; the Gaussian jitter in
\(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}\) is an implementable vanishing version
that does not require estimating the jump.  This proves both the
positive construction and the claimed necessity statement.
theorem.justification: External vanishing randomization converts the proved singular Gaussian approximation into exact, rather than merely conservative, null calibration.
theorem.gap: The same-sample estimated-plane correction is handled by the frozen influence expansion; the remaining atomic discontinuity is removed by an explicit vanishing Gaussian jitter.
theorem.consumer: The construction gives an implementable covariance-adaptive Anderson--Rubin confidence set for weak environmental cumulant flags.

proposed.name: randomized-jitter Gaussian-multiplier Anderson--Rubin inversion
proposed.construction:
Let
\[
 \mathcal K=\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\},
 \qquad
 q=(E-1)|\mathcal K|,
 \qquad
 \|x\|_{\max}=\max_{k\in\mathcal K}\|x_k\|_2
\]
for a vector \(x=(x_k:k\in\mathcal K)\in\mathbb R^q\).  Each coordinate of every sample cumulant is a fixed finite linear combination of symmetric \(U\)-statistics.  For an order-\(s\) constituent with kernel \(g\) in environment \(e\), define its leave-one-out first-projection estimate by
\[
 \widehat\psi_{g,e,i}
 =
 s\left[
 {n_e-1\choose s-1}^{-1}
 \sum_{\substack{J\subset\{1,\ldots,n_e\}\setminus\{i\}\\|J|=s-1}}
 g(W_{e,i},W_{e,J})-U_{e,s}(g)
 \right].
\]
Apply the same fixed linear combinations and the environment-versus-baseline contrast signs to obtain \(\widehat\psi^C_{e,i}\), \(\widehat\psi^c_{e,k,i}\), and \(\widehat\psi^m_{e,k,i}\).  Define
\[
 \widehat C^\dagger=
 \begin{cases}
  (\widehat C^\top\widehat C)^{-1}\widehat C^\top,
    &\sigma_d(\widehat C)\geq\kappa_0/2,\\
  0,&\sigma_d(\widehat C)<\kappa_0/2,
 \end{cases}
\]
and, for \(b\in[-B,B]\),
\[
 \widehat h_k(b)=\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k,
 \qquad
 \widehat\zeta_{e,k,i}(b)
 =
 \widehat Q\left\{
 \widehat\psi^m_{e,k,i}
 -b\widehat\psi^c_{e,k,i}
 -\widehat\psi^C_{e,i}\widehat C^\dagger\widehat h_k(b)
 \right\}.
\]
Let \(\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(b)\in\mathbb R^q\) stack these vectors over \(k\in\mathcal K\), and put
\[
 H_n(b)=
 \left(
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-b\widehat c_k):
 k\in\mathcal K
 \right).
\]
Set
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\},\qquad
 \rho=\frac{\nu}{8+4\nu},
\]
fix \(0<\chi<\rho\), let \(\tau_n=n^{-\chi}\), and choose an integer \(m_n\to\infty\).  Independently of the data, draw mutually independent standard normal multipliers
\[
 \{\omega^{(j)}_{e,i}:e\in\mathcal E,\ 1\leq i\leq n_e,\
 1\leq j\leq m_n\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \xi_0,\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{m_n}.
\]
For each \(b\in[-B,B]\), form
\[
 G^{*(j)}_n(b)
 =
 \frac1{\sqrt n}
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \pi_e^{-1}\widehat\zeta_{e,i}(b)\omega^{(j)}_{e,i},
\]
\[
 V_n(b)=\|H_n(b)\|_{\max}+\tau_n\xi_0,
 \qquad
 V^{*(j)}_n(b)=\|G^{*(j)}_n(b)\|_{\max}+\tau_n\xi_j,
\]
and the simulated upper-tail probability
\[
 \widehat p_{n,m_n}(b)
 =
 \frac1{m_n}\sum_{j=1}^{m_n}
 \mathbf 1\{V^{*(j)}_n(b)\geq V_n(b)\}.
\]
The randomized-jitter inversion is
\[
 \mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}
 =
 \{b\in[-B,B]:\widehat p_{n,m_n}(b)>\alpha_0\}.
\]
Equivalently, up to the empirical-quantile discrepancy of at most \(1/m_n\), accept \(b\) when \(V_n(b)\) does not exceed the empirical \((1-\alpha_0)\)-quantile of \(\{V_n^{*(j)}(b)\}_{j=1}^{m_n}\).  If an environment has fewer observations than a constituent \(U\)-statistic requires, set \(\mathcal C_n^{\mathrm{RJ}}=[-B,B]\); balanced shares make this fallback inactive for all sufficiently large \(n\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: Adds the explicit multiplier, covariance, jitter, Monte Carlo, and inversion map needed for an implementable answer to the open-ended question.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(r\in\{d+2,\ldots,R_{\max}\}\).  All constants below are independent of the member of the triangular array, and we suppress the array index \(n\) when no ambiguity results.  By the treatment-loading, effect, and confounding bounds,
\[
 |\alpha|\leq a_1,\qquad |\beta|\leq B,
 \qquad |\gamma|=|\alpha|\,|\gamma/\alpha|\leq a_1q_1.
\tag{1}
\]
For \(s=2R_{\max}+\delta\), the structural equations and the inequality
\[
 |x_1+\cdots+x_j|^s\leq j^{s-1}\sum_{a=1}^j|x_a|^s
\]
therefore turn the source moment envelope into a constant \(K_W<\infty\) such that
\[
 \sup_n\max_{e\in\mathcal E}
 \mathbb E\!\left[\|W_{e,1}\|^{2R_{\max}+\delta}\right]
 \leq K_W.
\tag{2}
\]
Balanced shares give \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\), so every environment sample size tends to infinity uniformly.  In particular, the small-sample fallback in the estimator definition is inactive for all sufficiently large \(n\).

For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_k\), the moment--cumulant formula is the finite polynomial
\[
 \kappa_k(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
 =\sum_{\mathcal P}
 (|\mathcal P|-1)!(-1)^{|\mathcal P|-1}
 \prod_{D\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E\!\left[\prod_{j\in D}X_j\right],
\tag{3}
\]
where \(\mathcal P\) ranges over the partitions of \(\{1,\ldots,k\}\).  Replacing every product of expectations in (3) by its symmetrized average over distinct observations is precisely the stipulated unbiased cumulant statistic.  Hence each coordinate of \(\widehat C\), \(\widehat c_k\), and \(\widehat m_k\) is a finite linear combination, with coefficients depending only on \(R_{\max}\), of symmetric \(U\)-statistics whose order and total polynomial degree do not exceed \(R_{\max}\).

We derive the required first-projection representation directly.  For a symmetric statistic \(U_s(g)\), recursively subtract from \(g\) every conditional expectation involving fewer arguments, and denote the resulting centered canonical projections by \(g_j\), \(1\leq j\leq s\).  Inclusion--exclusion gives the exact identity
\[
 U_s(g)-\mathbb E g
 =\frac1{n_e}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\psi_g(W_{e,i})
  +\sum_{j=2}^s {s\choose j}U_j(g_j),
 \qquad
 \psi_g(w)=s\bigl(\mathbb E[g(w,W_2,\ldots,W_s)]-\mathbb E g\bigr).
\tag{4}
\]
Each \(g_j\) in the second sum has conditional mean zero in every argument.  Thus two terms indexed by distinct unordered \(j\)-tuples have zero covariance unless their tuples are identical, whence
\[
 \mathbb E[U_j(g_j)^2]
 \leq {n_e\choose j}^{-1}\mathbb E[g_j^2]
 \leq K n_e^{-j}.
\tag{5}
\]
The final bound is uniform by (2), because all kernels have total polynomial degree at most \(R_{\max}\).  There are only finitely many coordinates and partitions.  Stack (4), apply (5), and insert the signs defining the environment-versus-baseline contrasts.  This constructs centered first-projection arrays \(\psi^C_{e,n}\), \(\psi^c_{e,k,n}\), and \(\psi^m_{e,k,n}\) for which
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat C-C)
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
   \pi_e^{-1}\psi^C_{e,n}(W_{e,i})+o_{L^2}(1),
\tag{6}
\]
with analogous formulas for \(\sqrt n(\widehat c_k-c_k)\) and \(\sqrt n(\widehat m_k-m_k)\), simultaneously over \(2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\).  All remainders in (6) are uniform because the right side of (5), after multiplication by \(n\), is \(O(n^{-1})\) for every \(j\geq2\), using \(n_e\geq\underline\pi n\).

Put
\[
 \nu=\min\{1,\delta/R_{\max}\}>0.
\]
Since \((2+\nu)R_{\max}\leq2R_{\max}+\delta\), (2) and the polynomial-degree bound for the first projections also imply
\[
 \sup_{n,e}\mathbb E\!\left[
 \|\psi^C_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 +\sum_{k=2}^{R_{\max}}
 \left(\|\psi^c_{e,k,n}\|^{2+\nu}
       +\|\psi^m_{e,k,n}\|^{2+\nu}\right)
 \right]<\infty.
\tag{7}
\]

We next account for estimation of \(A\).  Let \(P_C=CC^+\), where \(C^+=(C^\top C)^{-1}C^\top\), so \(Q_A=I-P_C\).  If \(H\) perturbs \(C\), direct expansion of the displayed formula for \(P_C\) yields
\[
 P_{C+H}-P_C
 =Q_AHC^+ +(Q_AHC^+)^\top+R_C(H),
 \qquad \|R_C(H)\|\leq K_P\|H\|^2
\tag{8}
\]
whenever \(\|H\|\leq\kappa_0/2\).  Indeed, with \(G=C^\top C\) and \(D=C^\top H+H^\top C+H^\top H\),
\[
 (G+D)^{-1}=G^{-1}-G^{-1}DG^{-1}
 +G^{-1}DG^{-1}D(G+D)^{-1}.
\tag{9}
\]
The calibration gap gives \(\|G^{-1}\|\leq\kappa_0^{-2}\); the cumulant polynomial (3) and (2) uniformly bound \(\|C\|\); and the same gap plus \(\|H\|\leq\kappa_0/2\) uniformly bounds the last inverse in (9).  After multiplication by \(C+H\) and \((C+H)^\top\), the linear terms in (9) are exactly the two displayed linear terms in (8), and every remaining term contains at least two factors of \(H\).  This proves the uniform remainder bound in (8).

Equation (6) gives \(\|\widehat C-C\|=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\) uniformly.  Thus the event needed for (8) has probability tending uniformly to one; on it \(\widehat C\) has rank \(d\), and the rank-\(d\) SVD projector in the estimator definition equals \(I-P_{\widehat C}\).  Taking \(H=\widehat C-C\) in (8) gives
\[
 \widehat Q-Q_A
 =-Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+
  -\bigl(Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\bigr)^\top
  +o_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})
\tag{10}
\]
uniformly.

For each \(k\), put \(h_k=m_k-\beta c_k\).  The already-established cumulant-cancellation lemma gives
\[
 h_k\in A=\operatorname{col}(C),\qquad Q_Ah_k=0.
\tag{11}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \bigl(Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+\bigr)^\top h_k
 =C^{+\top}(\widehat C-C)^\top Q_Ah_k=0.
\tag{12}
\]
The cumulant formula (3), the coefficient bounds (1), and the moment bound (2) uniformly bound \(h_k\).  Combining (6), (10), (11), and (12), while using the fact that a product of two uniformly root-\(n\) estimation errors is \(O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1})\), gives, simultaneously for \(d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sqrt n\,\widehat Q(\widehat m_k-\beta\widehat c_k)
 &=\sqrt n\,Q_A\bigl[(\widehat m_k-m_k)
       -\beta(\widehat c_k-c_k)\bigr]
   -\sqrt n\,Q_A(\widehat C-C)C^+h_k+o_{\mathbb P}(1)\\
 &=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}\pi_e^{-1}
 Q_A\bigl(\psi^m_{e,k,n}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k,n}
            -\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\bigr)(W_{e,i})
 +o_{\mathbb P}(1).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
This is the claimed expansion with
\[
 \zeta_{e,k,n}=Q_A\bigl(\psi^m_{e,k,n}-\beta\psi^c_{e,k,n}
 -\psi^C_{e,n}C^+h_k\bigr),
\]
and it displays the same-sample estimated-plane correction explicitly.

It remains to prove the uniform Gaussian approximation without imposing nonsingularity.  Let \(\zeta_{e,n}\) be the stack of \(\zeta_{e,k,n}\) over \(d+2\leq k\leq R_{\max}\).  The bounds (1), (7), and (11), together with \(\|Q_A\|\leq1\) and \(\|C^+\|\leq\kappa_0^{-1}\), imply
\[
 \sup_{n,e}\mathbb E\|\zeta_{e,n}\|^{2+\nu}<\infty.
\tag{14}
\]
Define independent centered summands
\[
 X_{e,i,n}=n^{-1/2}\pi_e^{-1}\zeta_{e,n}(W_{e,i}).
\]
By balanced shares and (14),
\[
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \mathbb E\|X_{e,i,n}\|^{2+\nu}
 \leq K n^{-\nu/2}\longrightarrow0
\tag{15}
\]
uniformly.  Their covariance sum is exactly
\[
 \sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\sum_{i=1}^{n_e}
 \mathbb E[X_{e,i,n}X_{e,i,n}^\top]
 =\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}\pi_e^{-1}
 \mathbb E[\zeta_{e,n}\zeta_{e,n}^\top]=\Sigma_n.
\tag{16}
\]
For each fixed vector \(t\), Taylor expansion of \(\exp(i t^\top X_{e,i,n})\) through order two has absolute expected remainder at most \(K_t\mathbb E\|X_{e,i,n}\|^{2+\nu}\).  Independence, (15), and (16) therefore give
\[
 \mathbb E\exp(i t^\top Z_n)
 -\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12t^\top\Sigma_nt\right)\longrightarrow0
\tag{17}
\]
uniformly.

Finally, (14) makes \(\{\Sigma_n\}\) a bounded subset of the fixed-dimensional positive-semidefinite cone.  If the asserted uniform bounded-Lipschitz convergence failed, a violating sequence would have a subsequence on which \(\Sigma_n\to\Sigma\) for some positive-semidefinite \(\Sigma\).  On this subsequence, (17) and the continuity theorem for characteristic functions yield \(Z_n\Rightarrow N(0,\Sigma)\), while \(N(0,\Sigma_n)\Rightarrow N(0,\Sigma)\).  Since the bounded-Lipschitz metric metrizes weak convergence on Euclidean space, the triangle inequality then forces
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\!\left(\mathcal L(Z_n),N(0,\Sigma_n)\right)\longrightarrow0,
\]
contradicting the choice of the sequence.  No inverse of \(\Sigma_n\) was used.  Thus the argument covers singular \(\Sigma_n\), in which case the Gaussian is supported on \(\operatorname{im}(\Sigma_n)\), and proves every assertion of the lemma.
